articles.title: Anatomical Handling Properties of Costal and Auricular Cartilage in Fresh-frozen Cadaveric Models for Revision Rhinoplasty.
articles.authors: Francesca Russo, Sebastiano Grimaldi, Giuseppe Esposito et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Revision rhinoplasty is among the most technically demanding procedures in facial surgery, requiring mastery of complex anatomy, advanced surgical skills, and proficiency in structural grafting. Cadaveric dissection remains a fundamental component of surgical training, yet the suitability of fresh-frozen anatomical specimens for simulating graft preparation has not been systematically assessed. This study evaluates the handling characteristics and graft-preparation feasibility of costal and auricular cartilage harvested from fresh-frozen cadavers used in structured revision rhinoplasty dissection. METHODS: Ten fresh-frozen cadaveric heads and two thoracic specimens were dissected. Costal cartilage was harvested bilaterally from ribs 5-8, and auricular cartilage bilaterally through a posterior conchal approach. Graft length, width, thickness, preparation time, carvability, laminar fragmentation, and suturability were assessed. Because multiple samples were obtained from the same donor, donor-level means were used for inferential comparisons. RESULTS: Costal cartilage was rigid and brittle, with macroscopic and handling characteristics consistent with calcification. Laminar thinning resulted in fragmentation in 85% of attempts, and intentionally thicker slices displayed macroscopically visible microfractures and fractured during suturing. No costal graft was suitable for spreader or septal extension graft simulation. Auricular cartilage maintained elasticity, allowed reproducible laminar carving, and withstood suturing without fracture. Preparation time differed significantly between graft types. CONCLUSION: In the specimens examined, costal cartilage was unsuitable for laminar graft-preparation simulation because of fragmentation and fracture, although rib harvesting remained valuable for thoracic-exposure training. Auricular cartilage was more consistently suitable for graft-shaping simulation. These findings describe distinct roles for the two cartilage sources within fresh-frozen cadaveric simulation of revision rhinoplasty.

articles.title: Branch-level anatomy and estimated portal injury risk during anterior ankle arthroscopy: a combined ultrasound and cadaveric study.
articles.authors: Hannes Platzgummer, Tobias Smodics, Veronika Vetchy et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To map the nerve branches at risk at the anterior ankle joint line with ultrasound, validate them by dissection, measure branch-specific distances to the anterolateral and anteromedial portals, and estimate per-branch injury probability. METHODS: Fourteen fresh-frozen ankles from 7 body donors were examined with high-resolution ultrasound (10-22 MHz). The intermediate (NCDI) and medial (NCDM) dorsal cutaneous nerves, the deep fibular nerve and the saphenous nerve were identified at the anterior joint line, dye-marked and verified by dissection. Distances to the portals were measured with digital calipers; injury probability was estimated with a normal distribution model and bootstrap confidence intervals. RESULTS: Dissection confirmed all sonographically identified branches (saphenous nerve 13/14 specimens, all others 14/14). The NCDI was single in 57% of specimens and split into two sub-branches in 43%. The single NCDI lay 3.6 ± 10.3 mm from the anterolateral portal (1-mm risk 3.6%, 4-mm risk 14.4%); each split sub-branch carried 5.6% and 22.1%, respectively. The saphenous nerve lay - 5.7 ± 5.2 mm from the anteromedial portal (1-mm risk 4.2%, 4-mm risk 17.0%). The NCDM and deep fibular nerve carried a 4-mm risk of 4.0% or less. The combined risk at either portal was 8.7% at 1-mm incision and 32.5% at 4-mm trocar width. CONCLUSIONS: Anterior ankle portal risk is branch-specific: in 43% of specimens, two NCDI sub-branches cross the anterolateral portal field. The combined 4-mm estimate reflects nerve contact rather than clinical injury and is an upper estimate. High-resolution ultrasound identified all sub-branches verified at dissection and may support preoperative portal planning.

articles.title: Bilateral asymmetric accessory iliopsoas musculature and variant relationships with the femoral nerve: an anatomical case report.
articles.authors: Caitlin Wetzel, Bailey Hall, Keirsten Templin et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Accessory musculature within the interval between the psoas major and iliacus may alter the expected course of the femoral nerve and complicate imaging or surgical exposure. This report describes a rare bilateral but asymmetric configuration of accessory iliopsoas musculature. METHODS: The posterior abdominal wall and iliopsoas regions of an 85-year-old male whole-body donor were dissected bilaterally. Accessory muscle origins, distal fusion patterns, dimensions, and relationships with the femoral nerve were documented. RESULTS: Two accessory muscular heads were identified on each side. On the left, both arose from the L4 costal process; on the right, the heads arose separately from the L2 and L3 costal processes. One head on each side fused to the native psoas major, and the other to the native iliacus. The femoral nerve passed between the native psoas major and accessory psoas-associated head on the left, but between the two accessory heads on the right. The heads differed in length and caliber between sides. CONCLUSION: In this donor, bilateral accessory iliopsoas heads had different origins and femoral nerve relationships. Recognition of unexpected intermuscular nerve intervals may aid anatomical interpretation and operative orientation, particularly in posterior abdominal wall or retroperitoneal exposures. No evidence of femoral neuropathy or altered biomechanical function was available.

articles.title: Does the morphology of the mandibular lingula affect the location of the mandibular foramen?
articles.authors: Atapol Yongvikul, Manop Khanijou, Nattharin Wongsirichat et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Accurate localization of the mandibular foramen (MF) is essential for successful inferior alveolar nerve block. The mandibular lingula (ML), a bony projection partially overlying the MF, is commonly used as an anatomical landmark; however, its morphology exhibits considerable variation. This study aimed to evaluate the relationship between ML morphology and the spatial position of the MF using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). METHODS: This retrospective CBCT-based study analyzed 288 scans (144 females; mean age 51.0 ± 19.4 years) acquired between March 2023 and March 2025. ML morphology was classified into truncated, nodular, assimilated, and other types. Vertical and horizontal relationships between the ML, MF, mandibular borders, and oblique ridges were measured using multiplanar reconstruction. MF dimensions and the presence of accessory mandibular canals were also assessed. Inter- and intra-examiner reliability were evaluated. Statistical analysis included one-way ANOVA and independent t-tests, with significance set at P < 0.05. RESULTS: The nodular ML was the most prevalent morphology (60.76%). ML type did not significantly influence the vertical position or dimensions of the MF (P > 0.05). However, significant differences were observed in horizontal localization, particularly relative to the internal oblique ridge, with the assimilated ML type demonstrating a more posteriorly positioned MF (P < 0.05). Accessory mandibular canals, present in 5.56% of cases, were associated with significantly reduced horizontal distances to the MF. CONCLUSION: ML morphology significantly influences its horizontal localization. Assimilated lingula and accessory mandibular canals may compromise the reliability of conventional landmarks.

articles.title: Morphological variability of the last denticulate ligament process: an anatomical study.
articles.authors: Loris Chaboissier, Ilona Baffaleuf, Hugo Lecot et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The denticulate ligament plays a role in stabilizing the spinal cord. Its most distal extension, the last denticulate ligament process (LDLP), remains poorly described in the literature. This study aims to provide a comprehensive morphological characterization of the LDLP and its anatomical relationships. METHOD: Forty-four cadaveric dissections were performed, allowing analysis of 87 LDLPs. A posterior approach with intermyolaminar dissection between vertebral levels T10 and L4 was used. Morphological parameters and precise measurements, including distances between the LDLP and the apex of the conus medullaris, were recorded. The adjacent sensory rootlets were systematically documented. RESULTS: Five distinct LDLP morphologies were identified: long oblique, short oblique, horizontal, bifid, and atypical. The denticulate ligament terminated in a slender, pearly filament located cranial to the filum terminale. The LDLP was most frequently observed at the T12-L1 level (40.2%) and adjacent to L3 sensory rootlets (66.6%). The caudal spinal insertion of the LDLP was on average 4.34 cm from the apex of the conus medullaris. A notable positional trend was observed: on average, when the conus medullaris was located at vertebral level L1 or lower, the LDLP was positioned one vertebral level higher; specifically, when the conus medullaris was located at T12-L1, the LDLP was most frequently found at the T12 level. CONCLUSION: The LDLP displayed five morphological patterns and variable vertebral levels, with most insertions located around T12-L1. Its consistent relationships with the conus medullaris and sensory rootlets may provide useful anatomical landmarks for neurosurgical procedures.

articles.title: Distinguishing anatomical complexity from clinical risk in dual-origin lingual artery anatomy.
Identifying specific brain morphology modes affecting brain strain under head impact.
articles.authors: Yihan Zhang, Xiaoyu Du, Jingyi Wu et al.
articles.abstract: Head impacts induce head accelerations that generate brain strain and may ultimately lead to traumatic brain injury (TBI). Although previous studies have shown that brain morphology influences strain responses, it remains unclear which specific morphology modes are biomechanically relevant, whether their effects are consistent across strain metrics, and where these effects occur within the brain. In this study, we established 37 Brain Morphology Modes (BMMs), which explained 90.14 % of population-level morphological variation, and represented each individual brain using a corresponding set of Brain Morphology Signature (BMS) scores. Using synthetic brain models under controlled kinematics and subject-specific brain models under real-world head impacts, we found that the relationships between BMMs and brain strain responses varied across morphology modes, strain metrics, and brain regions, exhibiting morphology-dominant, direction-dependent, or mixed contribution patterns. These findings indicate that morphology-related brain strain variation cannot be explained solely by global geometric scaling, but also depends on mode-specific morphology-kinematics interactions.

articles.title: Effects of Exercise on Symptom Burden During Cancer Treatment: Real-World Evidence from a Statewide Exercise Oncology Program.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Hao Luo, Robert U Newton, Dennis R Taaffe et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Cancer treatment often exacerbates symptoms such as fatigue, insomnia, and gastrointestinal disturbances. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence of exercise on symptom control in patients undergoing cancer treatment. METHODS: The analysis included patients undergoing cancer treatment, who participated in the three-month Life Now Exercise oncology program across 13 community-based sites in Western Australia. Individually tailored resistance, aerobic, and flexibility exercises at a moderate-to-high intensity were delivered twice per week in a group format, supervised by accredited exercise physiologists. Symptom burden was assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and six months post-intervention using the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality-of-Life Core module (EORTC QLQ-C30) and the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue scale (FACIT-F). RESULTS: Of 328 participants, 63% were aged under 65 years, 56% had breast cancer, 86% had localised disease, and 60% were undergoing hormonal therapy with/without additional radiotherapy and other systemic therapies. Improvements were observed at post-intervention in fatigue (EORTC: -3.3 [95% CI -5.5 to -1.1]; FACIT-F: 1.7 [95% CI 0.7 to 2.7]), insomnia (-3.6 [95% CI -6.9 to -0.3]), appetite loss (-3.2 [95% CI -5.9 to -0.5]), and financial difficulties (-2.8 [95% CI -5.5 to -0.1]), with most improvements sustained at six months post-intervention. Responses varied across breast, digestive, and genitourinary cancer subgroups and were associated with diverse demographic and clinical factors. However, meaningful improvements were consistently observed in patients with clinically relevant symptoms at baseline. CONCLUSIONS: Multimodal exercise at a moderate-to-high intensity is a promising non-pharmaceutical intervention for reducing symptom burden during cancer treatment. Similar exercise programs may be considered during cancer treatment for symptom control.

articles.title: Female anatomies disguise ECG abnormalities following myocardial infarction: An artificial intelligence-enabled modelling and simulation study.
articles.authors: Hannah Joy Smith, Leto Luana Riebel, Ruben Doste et al.
articles.abstract: The ECG is modulated by torso-heart anatomy, challenging patients' diagnosis and risk stratification. This study aims to quantify how torso-heart anatomical factors affect sex differences in ECG biomarkers in acute and chronic myocardial infarction (MI). We exploit the perfect control of artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented multiscale modelling and simulation, using clinical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ECGs for model construction and validation. A cohort of 1720 torso-ventricular anatomies (50% female) was constructed from MRIs of healthy and post-MI participants in the UK Biobank. A total of 8600 simulations were performed considering anatomical variability, three electrophysiological stages (healthy, ischaemic and infarcted) and two infarct locations (anteroseptal and inferolateral). Quantifying the effect of cardiac size, position and orientation on each ECG biomarker, we found that female anatomies had larger distances between infarct and ECG electrodes (relative to cardiac size) and larger angles between infarct normal and ECG lead axes, both primarily caused by their more superior cardiac position. This reduced ST elevation and amplitude of late depolarisation and repolarisation tails, ultimately shortening QRS duration (QRSd) and T-peak-to-end interval (TpTe). Overall, position and orientation of the heart impacted TpTe more severely than QRSd; our AI-enabled mechanistic modelling and simulation identified smaller ventricles, superior cardiac position and different ventricular orientation as key anatomical contributors of QRSd, TpTe and ST elevation being reduced in female versus male anatomies. Our framework provides a blueprint for quantifying the impact of anatomical sex differences on functional markers and enables future work in tailoring clinical guidelines considering unique patient anatomy to reduce biased outcomes. KEY POINTS: The ECG, important in diagnosing and managing treatment for myocardial infarction (heart attacks), is known to be impacted by the anatomy of the heart and torso. Women suffering myocardial infarction are underdiagnosed, and the effect of anatomical sex differences on the ECG in myocardial infarction is poorly understood. Our human computational modelling and simulation demonstrate that ST elevation in ischaemia was reduced in female anatomies, mainly as their hearts are higher in the torso than male anatomies. We show that ECG time intervals were affected differently by anatomy: the T-peak-to-end interval was more sensitive to cardiac positioning, whereas QRS duration was more sensitive to cardiac size. Our study demonstrates how computer simulations provide an efficient mechanistic tool to quantify the role of anatomical differences in clinical biomarkers and could ultimately support the inclusion of sex differences in clinical guidelines.

articles.title: Intermittent vagus nerve stimulation elicits spinal serotonin-dependent phrenic motor facilitation.
articles.authors: Alec L E Butenas, Gordon S Mitchell
articles.abstract: Intermittent vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) elicits a persistent increase in phrenic motor output, termed phrenic motor facilitation (pMF). However, prior studies demonstrating VNS-induced pMF used high-frequency stimulation (50 Hz), above the discharge frequencies of most afferent fibres. Here, we tested the hypothesis that 15, 1-min episodes of low-frequency (5 Hz; ∼6 V; 5 ms pulse width) VNS evoke pMF in urethane-anaesthetized, neuromuscularly blockaded and ventilated male rats; we also studied ∼4- vs. ∼16-month-old rats to assess the impact of advancing age. Low-frequency VNS elicited robust pMF for at least 90 min in young rats (n = 7); at 90 min post-stimulation, VNS increased integrated phrenic burst amplitude by 49% (±18% SD) vs. 17% (±15% SD) in time controls (n = 7; P = 0.004). We also tested whether VNS elicits long-term facilitation in renal sympathetic nerve activity; facilitation was not observed. We compared afferent vs. efferent VNS (cut nerves; each n = 7); afferent, not efferent, stimulation elicited pMF. Cervical intrathecal 5-HT2 receptor antagonism blocked VNS-induced pMF; neither 5-HT7 nor α1-adrenergic receptor antagonism had significant effects (n = 7 each). Since VNS activates slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors, we tested whether intermittent positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) evokes pMF. Intermittent PEEP elicited significant pMF (n = 7), implicating pulmonary stretch receptors as contributors to VNS-induced pMF. In ∼16-month-old rats (n = 5), neither phrenic nor renal sympathetic nerve facilitation was observed following intermittent VNS. Thus, low-frequency VNS is a robust stimulus to respiratory motor plasticity in young male rats. Slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors and spinal 5-HT2 receptors play important roles in its underlying mechanism.

articles.title: Time-Restricted Eating and Caloric Restriction Impact Bone and the Gut Microbiota in Postmenopausal Women: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Brandon D McGuire, Shreya Ghosh, Yvette Schlussel et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Caloric restriction (CR) can reduce bone mineral density (BMD). Time-restricted eating (TRE) modulates circadian rhythms and gut microbiota, but its effects on bone when combined with CR are unknown. OBJECTIVES: This study examined the effects of TRE+CR on bone in postmenopausal females with overweight or obesity and whether it is associated with changes in the gut microbiota. METHODS: Forty-nine postmenopausal females (body mass index ≥25 kg/m2, 50-79 years) were randomized to 24-weeks of CR (-500 kcal/d) or TRE (<9-h eating)+CR. BMD and bone quality were assessed at weeks 0 and 24. Fecal samples were collected at weeks 0, 12, and 24, and blood samples at weeks 0 and 24. RESULTS: Participants (61±5 years, 33±4 kg/m2) had an eating window of 12.3±0.9 hours/day, which was maintained in the CR group (n=21) [+0.3h/day (0.0,0.68)], and reduced in the TRE+CR group (n=26) [-4.0h/day (-4.4,-3.6)] (P<0.001), with 88% and 94% adherence, respectively. Hip BMD decreased similarly in both groups over time [-0.010g/cm2 (-0.018, -0.002)] (P=0.001), without between-group differences (P=0.98). TRE+CR attenuated radius BMD loss compared to CR [0.009g/cm2 (-0.002, 0.021) vs. [-0.020g/cm2 (-0.033, -0.007); (P=0.001)]. Gut microbiota (beta-diversity) shifted within TRE+CR from baseline to week 24 (P<0.05), with increasing dissimilarity from the CR group emerging by week 12 (P<0.0001). Changes in microbial guild ratios were positively correlated with changes in radius BMD (P<0.05). Subgroup analysis indicated baseline microbial guilds predicted radius BMD preservation (AUC=0.73; 0.54, 0.92). Weight decreased [-6.8kg (-8.3, -5.4)] similarly between the groups (P=0.29), but visceral adiposity decreased more with TRE+CR (P=0.01). Serum bone turnover markers were unchanged, while glycemic indices improved (P<0.05) without between-group differences. CONCLUSIONS: TRE mitigated weight-loss-induced bone loss at a clinically relevant non-weight-bearing site, but not at the hip, and these effects may be associated with changes in the gut microbiota. Larger studies are needed to establish mechanisms and sustained health effects.

articles.title: Nutritional monitoring during spaceflight: tracking body composition and three-dimensional shape across a five-day research expedition.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Jonathan P Bennett, Michael C Wong, Nisa N Kelly et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Microgravity during spaceflight leads to rapid muscle loss and fluid shifts driven by skeletal unloading and dietary changes. Obtaining accurate measurements before, during, and after missions remains challenging due to the cost and feasibility limitations of traditional imaging and laboratory systems. OBJECTIVE: This study quantified changes in whole-body and regional body shape using three-dimensional optical imaging (3DO) and body composition using bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) before, during, and after a short-duration spaceflight. METHODS: Fat-free mass (FFM) and fat mass (FM) were estimated by combining 3DO-derived body volume (BV) and BIA-derived total body water (TBW) within a five-compartment (5C) model. Ground-based measurements were obtained immediately pre- and post-flight using clinically validated 3DO and BIA systems. In-flight assessments used smartphone-based 3DO and smartwatch-based BIA, calibrated to ground systems. Absolute and proportional changes in body mass, circumferences, and 5C body composition were characterized as the difference between post- and pre-flight values, with in-flight measures used to monitor longitudinal changes in TBW and body shape. RESULTS: Four astronauts completed the five-day research expedition. Body mass decreased by -2.27 ± 1.66 kg, driven primarily by FFM loss (-2.17 ± 1.22 kg), representing a -4.36 ± 2.76% proportional reduction (range: -1.12 to -7.76%). In-flight TBW reductions reached -3.0 L. Post-flight circumferences decreased across all regions, with the largest proportional changes in the legs and torso. The portable 5C approach demonstrated feasibility for in-mission monitoring, capturing rapid TBW loss confirmed by incomplete recovery upon landing. CONCLUSION: Alterations in diet, activity, and microgravity contributed to greater than 4% FFM loss over five days, with the greatest regional changes in the legs and torso. In-flight monitoring captured TBW loss that did not fully recover upon landing, demonstrating the feasibility of portable body composition monitoring for astronaut health management.

articles.title: Changes in energy availability, nutritional status, and physiological health across training phases in elite Chinese artistic swimmers.
articles.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
articles.authors: Xiangxin Li, Yan Chen, Yuxuan Wang et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Low energy availability (LEA) adversely affects athletes'physiological health, yet studies in elite synchronized swimmers across different pre-competition training phases are scarce. This study evaluated changes in energy availability, nutritional status, and physiological health in Chinese elite female synchronized swimmers before the National Games. METHODS: Ten Chinese elite female synchronized swimmers sequentially completed a 1-week tapering phase (TP) and a 4-week intensified training phase (ITP). At the end of each phase, dietary intake (weighed food records), exercise energy expenditure (heart rate monitoring), energy availability (EA), resting metabolic rate (RMR), body composition, and blood biomarkers were measured. Within each training phase, athletes were classified into LEA and non-LEA groups according to their EA levels, and between-group differences were compared. In addition, overall changes between TP and ITP were analyzed in the full cohort of 10 athletes. RESULTS: LEA prevalence was 40% during the TP and 60% during the ITP. In unadjusted analyzes, the LEA group showed significantly lower EI (p = 0.025), VO₂ (p = 0.022), mRMR (p = 0.023), RMR ratio (p = 0.006), and intakes of carbohydrate (p = 0.023), protein (p = 0.015), fat (p = 0.032), calcium (p = 0.038), and iron (p = 0.044) during the TP, with large effect-size estimates. As expected from the classification criteria, EA was significantly lower in the LEA group during both the TP (p = 0.001) and ITP (p = 0.005). During the ITP, fat (p = 0.027) and zinc intakes (p = 0.036) were significantly lower in the LEA group, whereas carbohydrate and protein intakes were lower but did not reach statistical significance. In the overall cohort, EEE (p < 0.001) and T4 (p = 0.010) increased from TP to ITP, whereas ferritin (p = 0.012) and calcium intake (p = 0.007) decreased, with large effect-size estimates. CONCLUSION: During intensified training, EEE increased without a corresponding increase in EI, suggesting that dietary intake may not have adequately matched the increased training demands and may have increased susceptibility to LEA. LEA was associated with lower energy and macronutrient intakes, potential calcium and iron inadequacies, and phase-specific reductions in RMR-related measures. Phase-related biomarker changes could not be attributed specifically to LEA. Individualized and periodized nutritional monitoring and intervention are recommended to better align energy and nutrient intake with training demands and support athlete health and performance.

articles.title: Effects of dietary nitrate supplementation in team sport athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
articles.authors: Mikołaj Szymocha, Paulina M Nowaczyk, Jakub Adamczewski et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Dietary nitrate (NO3 -), typically provided as beetroot juice, increases nitric oxide availability and may reduce the oxygen cost of exercise, improve muscle oxygenation, and delay fatigue. Evidence in team sport athletes, however, remains limited and has not been comprehensively synthesized. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluate the effects of NO3 - supplementation on team sport-specific performance and related physiological and biochemical outcomes. METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO CRD42022358739). PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through March 2025 for randomized, placebo-controlled trials investigating acute (single dose) or chronic (≥2 days, with the final dose taken 2-3 h before exercise) NO3 - supplementation in male or female team sport athletes. Effect sizes (Hedges' g) were synthesized using multilevel random-effects models (REML) with cluster-robust standard errors. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB 2.0 and certainty of evidence using GRADE. Robustness analyses, including sensitivity to assumed within-person correlations for crossover trials and Monte Carlo simulations to examine the stability of key contrasts under sparse evidence were performed. RESULTS: Twenty-four trials (n = 365 athletes; 277 males, 88 females) met inclusion criteria. Supplementation increased circulating and salivary NO3 -/NO2 -, indicating elevated systemic concentrations. The overall pooled ergogenic effect on performance was small but statistically significant (g = 0.075; 95% CI 0.026-0.124; p = 0.005). In team sport-specific tasks, NO3 - supplementation produced a small but consistent improvement with low heterogeneity and moderate certainty of evidence (g = 0.143; 95% CI 0.041-0.245; p = 0.011). A significant benefit was observed with chronic protocols (g = 0.145; 95% CI 0.076-0.214; p < 0.001), whereas acute protocols showed no clear effects. The chronic-acute contrast was statistically significant (g = 0.118; 95% CI 0.029-0.207; p = 0.013) but was not robust to more conservative crossover-correlation assumptions, lowering certainty to very low; because chronic protocols also included a final pre-exercise dose, this contrast should not be interpreted as evidence of long-term adaptation. Improvements were most evident in team sport-specific performance tests (moderate certainty), with additional, less certain signals in repeated high-intensity efforts and fatigue-sensitive neuromuscular outcomes (both very low certainty), while single-sprint outcomes and most metabolic/biochemical markers showed no consistent benefit. Cardiorespiratory responses were largely unchanged. Dose-response meta-regressions did not reveal consistent linear or non-linear trends. CONCLUSIONS: NO3 - supplementation provides small, context-dependent ergogenic benefits in team sport athletes, most consistently for team sport-specific performance (moderate certainty), with preliminary signals for repeated high-intensity efforts and fatigue-sensitive neuromuscular performance (both very low certainty). Evidence for moderation by protocol type, sex, and training status remains suggestive but uncertain and is currently insufficient to support specific dosing recommendations. Well-powered, standardized, sex-stratified trials with harmonized outcome measures are needed to clarify key moderators and strengthen applied guidance.

articles.title: Mindless eating as a behavioural correlate of addictive-like eating symptoms in 10-12-year-old children: associations with disordered eating attitudes.
articles.authors: Meliha Çavdar, Nilüfer Özkan, Büşra Aslan Gönül et al.
articles.abstract: Middle childhood is a critical developmental period for the emergence of eating-related self-regulatory processes and maladaptive eating patterns. This cross-sectional study of 1060 children aged 10-12 years examined associations among disordered eating attitudes, mindful eating dimensions and addictive-like eating symptoms, focusing on the indirect role of mindless eating. Data were collected using a socio-demographic form, the Mindful Eating Questionnaire for Children (MEQ-C), the dimensional Yale Food Addiction Scale for Children 2.0, the Stunkard Pictogram and the Children's Eating Attitudes Test. Correlation analyses were conducted to examine associations among variables. Multiple linear regression was used to examine variables independently associated with addictive-like eating symptoms. An exploratory indirect-effect model tested whether mindless eating was involved in the statistical association between disordered eating attitudes and addictive-like eating symptoms. BMI category and meal skipping showed significant multivariate effects. In the regression model, MEQ-C-Mindless Eating showed the strongest independent association with addictive-like eating symptoms (β = 0·556, p < 0·001), followed by BMI z-score (β = 0·167, p < 0·001), disordered eating attitudes (β = 0·115, p < 0·001) and meal skipping (β = -0·105, p < 0·001). The indirect-effect model suggested that the association between disordered eating attitudes and addictive-like eating symptoms was statistically consistent with an indirect association involving mindless eating. Mindless eating may be an important behavioural correlate of addictive-like eating symptoms in middle childhood and may help contextualise their association with disordered eating attitudes. These findings highlight the relevance of eating-related self-regulation in children, although the conceptual overlap between mindless eating and addictive-like eating measures suggests findings should be interpreted with some caution.
